opus-5.5.text:
I think the main challenge today is reliability. The capabilities are astonishing. These models can write code, reason through problems, and summarize huge amounts of information. But there's a big gap between a demo that works most of the time and a product people can depend on every time.

In many enterprise settings, being right 90% of the time isn't good enough. If you're automating a financial workflow, or a customer support process, or something touching production infrastructure, the cost of the 10% failure can wipe out the value of the 90%. And the failures are often unpredictable. You don't always know when the model will be wrong, and it doesn't always know either.

So much of the work now is less about the model and more about the system around it. How do you evaluate these systems properly? How do you combine models with verification, retrieval, tools, and human oversight so the overall system is more reliable than any single component? This is a familiar pattern from distributed systems. Individual machines fail, but you build systems that are reliable anyway. I think we need a similar discipline for AI: treat the model as a powerful but unreliable component and engineer around it.

There's also a practical side: cost and latency. Something that works great with the biggest model and lots of inference-time compute may not be economically viable at scale. Making these systems efficient, choosing the right model for the right task, and serving them well is a big part of turning capability into a product.

So in short, the capability is there. The hard part now is the engineering to make it dependable, measurable, and affordable.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts demos with dependable products but does not say that impressive demos lead people to overgeneralize AI’s capabilities.

r002.rationale: It says demos work “most of the time” and products must be dependable “every time”; it does not describe a demo needing only one impressive success.

r003.rationale: It discusses cost, efficiency, and choosing a model for a task, but does not identify selecting the use cases with the greatest business value as a challenge.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I'd say the main challenge is the gap between a demo and a product. It's remarkably easy today to build something that looks impressive, where the model answers a question or writes some code in a way that wows people. But a product needs to work reliably, every time, for real users, at a cost that makes sense. And that's where it gets hard.

A big part of it is that these models are inherently non-deterministic. If you ask the same question twice, you may get two different answers. Traditional software doesn't behave that way, and most of the engineering practices we've built up over decades, around testing, debugging, and guaranteeing correctness, assume deterministic behavior. So the question becomes: how do you build dependable systems on top of components that are, by nature, somewhat unpredictable?

The second challenge is evaluation. With traditional software, you write tests and you know whether it works. With LLM-based applications, it's often not obvious what "correct" even means, especially for open-ended tasks. If you can't measure quality, you can't improve it systematically, and you certainly can't promise anything to customers. That's actually a lot of what motivated our work on things like Chatbot Arena, because we needed better ways to assess these models in realistic settings.

And then there's cost and latency. Running these models is expensive, and if your product calls a large model multiple times per user request, the economics can fall apart quickly. So a lot of the practical work is about systems: routing between models of different sizes, caching, batching, deciding when a smaller or specialized model is good enough. That's very much a systems problem, and historically that's the kind of problem I've found most interesting.

So I'd summarize it this way: the capabilities are there, but turning them into value requires solving reliability, evaluation, and efficiency, and we're still in the early days of building the tooling and the discipline to do that well.

r001.rationale: The response says impressive demos can wow people, but does not say they cause people to overgeneralize what AI can do.

r002.rationale: It contrasts a demo that impresses with an answer to “a question” against a product that must work reliably “every time” for real users.

r003.rationale: It discusses reliability, evaluation, cost, and efficiency, but does not identify choosing the use cases with the greatest business value as a challenge.

astra-6.text:
I think the main challenge is closing the gap between something that works in a demo and something that works reliably for a customer. The model is a very important component, but it’s only one component. You need to connect it to the right data, integrate it into a workflow, and understand what happens when it makes a mistake.

And all of that has to work at a cost and latency that make sense. If you need a person to check every answer, that changes the economics. So the opportunity is to find applications where you can manage those errors and still deliver clear value. Start with a specific problem, measure whether you’re solving it, and improve the whole system—not just the model.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts demos with reliable customer products, but does not say impressive demos cause people to overgeneralize AI’s capabilities.

r002.rationale: It calls for reliability and handling mistakes, but does not distinguish succeeding on one impressive demo instance from working across all production cases.

r003.rationale: It recommends finding applications that manage errors and deliver clear value, but does not identify choosing the use cases with the greatest business value as the challenge.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the main challenge is closing the gap between something that works in a demo and something that works reliably for a customer. A demo can be impressive even if it fails occasionally. But if you put AI into a business process, you need to understand when it works, when it doesn’t, and what happens when it makes a mistake.

And reliability is only one dimension. You also have cost, latency, and integration with the customer’s data and existing systems. You have to solve all of these together while delivering enough value that someone is willing to pay for it.

So I would start with a concrete problem, define what success means, and build a way to measure it. The model is a very important component, but the product is the entire system around it.

r001.rationale: The response says demos can be impressive despite occasional failures, but does not say that people overgeneralize AI’s capabilities from them.

r002.rationale: It contrasts an impressive demo with reliable customer use, but does not make the specific distinction between one impressive successful instance and working across all cases.

r003.rationale: It recommends starting with a concrete problem and delivering enough value to earn payment, but does not identify selecting the use cases with the greatest business value as a challenge.
